tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
1	# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3
2	
3	Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.
4	
5	One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
6	one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
7	file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
8	`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.
9	
10	## Terminology
11	
12	Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
13	under it.
14	
15	- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
16	- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
17	  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
18	  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
19	  in any open thread.
20	- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
21	  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
22	  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
23	- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
24	- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
25	  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:

209	this block, bump the version-of-record, and rename the artifact to its dev name. It is also where
210	the trial begins: this file is created, and `TODO.md > ## In Progress` points at it.

212	##### feat: sync fetches only a repo with no local work
213	
214	A sync fetches whatever it is pointed at, and a fetch is where the damage is done: it moves a
215	bookmark that is behind, conflicts one that diverged, and rebases `@` onto a rewritten remote.
216	
217	- The gate is wink's: `@` empty, `@-` a commit on the remote, and every bookmark fast-forward
218	  only. Each names one way local work meets a fetch, and with none of them every commit a fetch
219	  can touch is the remote's own, so nothing can be lost and the way back is the old commit.
220	  - The agent-repo's `@` is not asked to be empty: it holds the running session's writes and
221	    never is. What that leaves open is a remote rewrite that touched the same session file, and
222	    there the sync stops with the state in place and rewinds nothing.
223	  - Local-only commits no bookmark names are left out. The work-repo holds three, the heads of
224	    bookmarks deleted this morning, and a check that counted them would hold the repo back for
225	    good over commits no sync moves.
226	- A held repo is not fetched at all, so there is nothing to restore: its remote-tracking refs are
227	  where they were, and the report lists what was found. The other repos still sync, and the run
228	  exits non-zero.
229	- `--rebase` is the go, widened from "rebase a non-empty `@` without asking" to "sync a repo that
230	  holds local work". The prompt on a terminal goes with it: the flag is the one way to say yes.
231	- The state is classified from the bookmark as it was before the fetch, since after it a repo
232	  that was behind reads as up to date.
233	- A fifth state, rewritten: the remote's commit replaced the local one and the fetch followed it,
234	  told from diverged by the bookmark already being on the remote's commit.
235	- An ahead bookmark is reported, where it was folded into "up to date, nothing to sync".
236	- What a held repo's report does not say is whether the remote moved too, sync not having asked
237	  it. Asking a remote for its head without fetching would add that, and is left for later.
238	
239	##### feat: sync --dry-run looks and changes nothing
240	
241	A held repo's report cannot say whether the remote moved too, and there is no way to learn what a
242	sync would do without running one. The look has to change nothing at all, a look that fetches and
243	restores being the design this cycle backed out of.
244	
245	- The remote is asked, not fetched: `git ls-remote <remote> refs/heads/<bookmark>` returns the
246	  commit the remote's bookmark is on, downloading and writing nothing.
247	- The call is a spawn of `git`, which the project bans, and wink reopened the spawn register for
248	  it as a sixth entry, temporary.
249	  - The first draft was written as if a spawn were ordinary here, the project spawning `jj -V`,
250	    `gh`, and an editor. Those are the register's named exceptions, and clippy stopped the build.
251	  - jj-lib is the reason the spawn is ours. It uses gix for a repo's local git store and spawns
252	    git itself for every network leg, keeps that layer `pub(crate)`, and builds gix with no
253	    network client, in 0.45.1 and in 0.46.0, read from the published source.
254	  - Turning on gix's network client was the other way to keep the ban whole, and was left: it
255	    would be the one path to a remote that is not jj-lib's, with its own transport and credential
256	    handling, so a look and the fetch after it could disagree.
257	  - The spawn runs the git executable jj's fetch runs, `git.executable-path`, and so takes the
258	    same config and credentials.
259	  - Three reminders make the exception findable when it can end: the register entry and the
260	    comment at the call, a `## Waiting` entry in `TODO.md`, and a note on the jj-lib line of
261	    `Cargo.toml` for whoever raises it.
262	- The state comes from three commits, the local bookmark, the remote's answer, and whether this
263	  repo has the remote's commit.
264	  - The repo has it: the two ancestry probes a sync makes, exact.
265	  - The repo does not: the remote moved to commits not yet fetched. A local bookmark that is on
266	    the remote holds nothing of its own, so a fetch would follow: behind. One that is not:
267	    diverged.
268	  - A remote that advanced and one that rewrote history read the same, behind, their commits
269	    not being here to tell apart. Only a fetch tells rewritten.
270	- The report is each repo's state, worded as what a sync would do, and the local work the gate
271	  would hold it back for.
272	- What it changes: nothing a sync cares about. The plan said "no jj operation, not even a
273	  snapshot", and that was too strong: "does `@` hold changes" is asked of the files, which takes
274	  the snapshot any jj command makes, and a repo with an edited file gains that one operation.
275	- It exits 0 whatever it found, a look that worked not being a failure.
276	- The report names the bookmark and ends each repo with a verdict, what a sync would do. Wink ran
277	  the first wording in iiac-perf, read "up-to-date" over an unpushed bookmark as "safe to sync",
278	  and it was not: the state is the synced bookmark's alone, and the gate would have held the
279	  repo back.

281	##### feat: sync tells a fast-forward from a rewrite
282	
283	The gate runs before any fetch and holds back every repo with local work, the one whose remote
284	has not moved and the one whose remote only added commits included. One unpushed bookmark
285	anywhere in a repo then stops every sync of it, wink's case in iiac-perf, and the look's verdict
286	there read "held back" over a `main` it had just called up to date.
287	
288	- Sync asks the remote where every one of its bookmarks is, a fetch bringing all of them, and
289	  compares with the last fetch. The remote where the last fetch left it means nothing to fetch:
290	  sync says so, notes the local work, and exits 0.
291	- When a bookmark moved, its commits are downloaded with no ref moved, and the move is classified
292	  by ancestry: a fast-forward, a rewrite, new, or deleted.
293	  - Tried in scratch repos, colocated and not: `git fetch --refmap= --no-tags
294	    --no-write-fetch-head <remote> <ref>` brought the remote's commit into the object store, left
295	    every git ref as it was, and jj saw nothing, no bookmark, `@`, or remote-tracking ref changed
296	    and no operation added, a later jj command included. `--refmap=` is what does it: without
297	    it git moves the remote-tracking ref as a side effect, and jj imports that as a fetch.
298	  - The ancestry walk is gix's, in-process: `rev_walk` is in the build as it is, where
299	    `merge_base` wants a feature jj-lib does not turn on. A revset cannot ask, jj not having
300	    imported the remote's commit.
301	  - It is a second form of the one spawn, under the same register entry, and both go through one
302	    function so the `#[allow]` is at one site.
303	- A fast-forward replaces nothing, so no local work can be moved by it: sync fetches, and says
304	  what it leaves untouched. Untouched is not brought up to date: an `@` with changes, or an
305	  unpushed bookmark, stays on the old commit, and moving it is the user's act.
306	- Two things still hold a repo back, each reported with its bookmark:
307	  - A bookmark that moved on the remote has local commits of its own, the fetch leaving it
308	    conflicted. This is any bookmark, not the synced one alone.
309	  - The remote rewrote or deleted a bookmark and the repo holds local work. Which commits the
310	    rewrite replaced is not worked out: any local work is taken as at risk, the check erring
311	    toward holding.
312	- The look and the sync share the finding out, `look_repos`, so the look's verdict and the sync's
313	  act cannot disagree. In the scratch scenarios each verdict was borne out by the sync run after
314	  it.
315	- A look now downloads, where the second rung's fetched nothing at all: the moved bookmarks'
316	  commits land in the git store with no ref naming them. They are the commits a fetch would
317	  bring.
318	- `--force` is the flag's documented name, wink's call, `--rebase` staying as an alias: past the
319	  gate there is often nothing to rebase, and "force a sync" is what the flag is reached for.
320	- Every sync now spawns git once to ask, and once more when the remote moved, where the look
321	  alone did.

324	
325	Closing out the cycle. Close-out shape: trapezoid.

327	- The cycle changed its design five times after it opened, and each change was found by trying
328	  the last one.
329	  - A dry run that put a bookmark back, a restore of the whole repo, a gate on local work alone,

336	  - A trial of the mechanism before the ladder is written would have found the first two faults
337	    in an hour: a fetch moves a bookmark, and a restore is blind to the remote afterwards.
338	- A project rule was learned by tripping it: the ban on spawning git, met when clippy stopped

343	  - A choice that changes what is pushed is worth restating in the words of its effect before

345	- The trial of this file is the subject of the Todo entry that makes it the rule, and what the

### feat: sync is safe by default

(wink, 2026-10-09) A `vc-x1 sync` fetches and then acts: a `main` that is behind is fast-forwarded,
one that diverged is rebased, and `@` is repositioned. An acquaint and a cycle start want to know a
repo is level without anything of theirs being put at risk, which today takes a `jj git fetch` and
a look.

- A sync is dangerous enough that its default guarantees, as best it can, that it messes nothing
  up, and that a neophyte can put things back the way they were before it.
- The agent runs it mid-conversation, and the user runs it with no agent to help, so the routine
  command neither rewinds a working copy nor leaves a state that needs interpreting.
- The parked agent-files v0.2.8 follows it, naming the look in its two steps.

#### Deliberation

- The record is in this file: a trial, on wink's word, of the planning and the work's
  documentation living apart from the backlog.
  - It bends [Cycle-record](AGENTS.md#cycle-record), which names `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. The
    bend covers where this cycle's block is written and its order, and nothing else: every other
    step of the protocol runs as the agent-files say.
  - The block opens with the Todo as picked, then the plan, the Ladder and its details, and the
    Deliberation last, the shape wink described: pick the Todo, move it here, and everything
    about the cycle is written under it.
  - `## Continuation notes` stays in `TODO.md` for now, since [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint)
    reads it there, and `TODO.md` keeps its `## In Progress` and `## Closed` headings, each
    pointing here.
  - This file holds one cycle, the one being worked on, and what comes next is in `TODO.md`,
    wink's rule. A `## Next` section was tried here for a day, holding the parked cycle and the
    planned one, and went back: planned work in two files was easy to lose track of.
- This cycle runs before agent-files v0.2.8, which is parked on its bookmark: its rule, "every
  cycle start syncs", is to name a sync that is safe to run unasked, and a rule written against
  the sync as it was would be rewritten a cycle later.
- The cycle grew twice before its first push, the shape still being free.
  - It opened as one commit, "feat: sync can look only, and asks on diverged", on a bookmark of
    that name, deleted unused.
  - A trial in scratch repos found the rewritten-remote case below, wink called the acting sync
    dangerous, and the default became "safe".
  - The `--undo` came in as a rung, wink's call over a cycle of its own, and went out again the
    next morning before any code, wink's call too: the cycle had grown long and tangled, the
    routine sync was safe without it, and its design held more than was left to give it. The
    design and its complications are kept in the Todo entry [sync --undo takes back the last
    sync](TODO.md#sync---undo-takes-back-the-last-sync).
  - The `--dry-run` came back as a rung of its own once it could be a look that fetches nothing.
  - A rung came in during the second work rung, "sync tells a fast-forward from a rewrite", from
    wink's trial of the look in iiac-perf.
  - Two rung titles were shortened before their push, having been written over the 50-character
    cap: "sync --dry-run asks the remote and changes nothing" and the new rung's first wording.
  - Five commits at the first push, six since. The plan was four with no separate opening, the
    first work rung carrying the setup, and wink had the opening inserted before the first push:
    the bookend pair exists, the cycle lands as an ordinary trapezoid, and the first work rung's
    diff is its work alone.
- A fetch is not a look, found by trial in scratch repos.
  - A tracked `main` that is behind is moved to the remote's, and one that diverged is left
    conflicted.
  - When the remote rewrote a commit the clone has, as a `squash-push` or an amended cycle
    bookmark does from another clone, the fetch rebases `@` onto the rewrite, and an edit in `@`
    to the same lines becomes conflict markers in the file on disk.
- The gate replaced three designs that each tried to undo a fetch after making it.
  - A `--dry-run` that put the bookmark back with a `bookmark set` missed the rewritten case: `@`
    had moved and the file held markers.
  - A restore to the pre-fetch operation that kept the remote-tracking refs left jj reading a
    rewritten remote as diverged from its own replacement, jj having already made its one follow.
  - A restore that also reset git's remote-tracking refs worked, and was dropped as the default
    on two points of wink's: a restore resets files on disk, and in the agent-repo those files are
    the conversation, and the user runs sync with no agent beside them to read a failure.
  - Not fetching needs none of it. The check is three reads of the repo, and what it refuses is
    exactly the work a fetch could hurt.
- No dry-run default: the bare command acts only where acting loses nothing. `--dry-run` is
  still wanted, wink's call, for what the gate cannot say: what the remote holds, and what a sync
  would do. It asks the remote and never fetches.
- The commit of the second work rung carries a legend line the rule does not have,
  ``Legend: `*` is a problem this commit addresses, `-` is a solution to it.``, on wink's word.
  - It bends [Commit-body form](agent-data/prose.md#commit-body-form), for that body and the
    bodies of this cycle's later rungs. The rule and its specimen are unchanged, the bodies
    pushed before it keep their form, and the change to the rule is the Todo entry [A commit
    body carries a legend for its markers](TODO.md#a-commit-body-carries-a-legend-for-its-markers).
  - The commit had been pushed without it, the agent having misread the go, and was
    re-described in both repos, each `ochid:` trailer kept, and force-pushed.
- A Todo entry was rewritten at the third work rung, [Scope is a flag on every
  command](TODO.md#scope-is-a-flag-on-every-command-and-push-resolves-its-own-bookmarks): wink
  tried `sync both` after `status both`, found the two disagree, and chose the flag for every
  command over the positional the entry had first decided on. Nothing in this cycle changes for
  it, `sync` taking its scope by `--scope` already.
- Two entries were added to `TODO.md` at the second rung: under `## Waiting`, the end of the git
  spawn, waiting on jj-lib, and under `## Todo`, [jj-lib moves to
  0.46.0](TODO.md#jj-lib-moves-to-0460), which wink found published while the spawn was weighed.
  - An upstream feature request for the query is wanted and not yet looked for.
- No marker bookmarks, wink's first thought for a way back: which commits a fetch will touch is
  not known before it runs, a bookmark pins a commit and not where the bookmarks, `@`, and the
  files were, and jj keeps every replaced commit in its operation log regardless.
- A held repo makes the run exit non-zero: the repo was not synced, and a `--quiet` caller has
  only the exit status to learn that from.
  - So an acquaint mid-cycle, the work-repo's `@` holding a rung's edits, reads a non-zero exit
    as the finding it already reports, uncommitted work.
  - It is a breaking change, and a patch, no minor having been named: a repo that is ahead, or
    that holds uncommitted changes, was synced before and is held back now.
- Stop-on-error stays as it was for the `--rebase` path: the state is left where the failing step
  stopped, with the operation ids printed.
- Two entries came along from the parked change so they reach `main`, both in `TODO.md`: the
  reworked `zDOING.md` entry and [TODO.md is renamed
  zTODO.md](TODO.md#todomd-is-renamed-ztodomd).
- The `## Waiting` entry's condition is unmet, `vc-x1 closed` not landed, so nothing promotes.

#### Solution

Before it fetches, a sync finds out what the fetch would do. It asks the remote where each of its
bookmarks is, downloads the commits of those that moved with no ref moved, and tells a
fast-forward from a rewrite. A remote that has not moved means nothing to fetch, and one that
only fast-forwarded is fetched with the repo's local work left where it is. A repo is held back,
not fetched and named in a failing exit, in two cases: a bookmark that moved has local commits of
its own, or the remote rewrote a bookmark and the repo holds local work. `--force` syncs it
anyway, `--rebase` being the same flag. With `--dry-run` the same finding out is reported and
nothing is moved, each repo ending with a verdict, what a sync would do.

A way to take back a forced sync, `--undo`, was planned here and deferred to a Todo entry.

#### Acceptance check

Run at the closing with the closing's build, in scratch clones of one bare remote, eight cases,
each a `--dry-run` and then the sync, by `tmp/accept-sync.sh`.

- In a scratch clone that is behind its remote and holds no local work, `vc-x1 sync`
  fast-forwards. Passed.
- In a scratch clone with an unpushed commit on `main` whose remote also moved, `vc-x1 sync`
  exits non-zero naming the repo and does not fetch, `main@origin` staying where it was, and
  `vc-x1 sync --force` rebases it. Passed, the unforced run exiting 1.
- In a scratch clone whose remote rewrote a commit, `vc-x1 sync` follows the rewrite when the repo
  holds no local work, and with an edited file in `@` it does not fetch and leaves the file
  untouched. Passed, the second exiting 1.
- In a scratch clone holding an unpushed bookmark, or uncommitted changes, `vc-x1 sync` succeeds
  when the remote has not moved, and when it fast-forwarded it moves `main` and leaves the local
  work where it was. Passed.
- In the same scratch clones, `vc-x1 sync --dry-run` reports the state and a verdict that the
  sync run after it bears out, and moves no bookmark, `@`, or remote-tracking ref. Passed, eight
  verdicts of eight borne out.
- In this workspace, `vc-x1 sync --scope=both --dry-run` reports both repos up to date with
  nothing to do, the work-repo's uncommitted changes noted. Passed.
- `vc-x1 validate` passes. Passed.

One check the opening stated was withdrawn with its rung: that `vc-x1 sync --undo` puts a forced
sync back and refuses when a commit was made since.

#### Ladder

- [feat: sync fetches only a repo with no local work][2] (done)
- [feat: sync --dry-run looks and changes nothing][3] (done)
- [feat: sync tells a fast-forward from a rewrite][4] (done)
- [feat: sync is safe by default closing][5] (done)

  - jj-lib is the reason the spawn is ours. It uses gix for a repo's local git store and spawns
    git itself for every network leg, keeps that layer `pub(crate)`, and builds gix with no
    network client, in 0.45.1 and in 0.46.0, read from the published source.
  - Turning on gix's network client was the other way to keep the ban whole, and was left: it
    would be the one path to a remote that is not jj-lib's, with its own transport and credential
    handling, so a look and the fetch after it could disagree.
  - The spawn runs the git executable jj's fetch runs, `git.executable-path`, and so takes the
    same config and credentials.
  - Three reminders make the exception findable when it can end: the register entry and the
    comment at the call, a `## Waiting` entry in `TODO.md`, and a note on the jj-lib line of
    `Cargo.toml` for whoever raises it.
- The state comes from three commits, the local bookmark, the remote's answer, and whether this
  repo has the remote's commit.
  - The repo has it: the two ancestry probes a sync makes, exact.
  - The repo does not: the remote moved to commits not yet fetched. A local bookmark that is on
    the remote holds nothing of its own, so a fetch would follow: behind. One that is not:
    diverged.
  - A remote that advanced and one that rewrote history read the same, behind, their commits
    not being here to tell apart. Only a fetch tells rewritten.
- The report is each repo's state, worded as what a sync would do, and the local work the gate
  would hold it back for.
- What it changes: nothing a sync cares about. The plan said "no jj operation, not even a
  snapshot", and that was too strong: "does `@` hold changes" is asked of the files, which takes
  the snapshot any jj command makes, and a repo with an edited file gains that one operation.
- It exits 0 whatever it found, a look that worked not being a failure.
- The report names the bookmark and ends each repo with a verdict, what a sync would do. Wink ran
  the first wording in iiac-perf, read "up-to-date" over an unpushed bookmark as "safe to sync",
  and it was not: the state is the synced bookmark's alone, and the gate would have held the
  repo back.

##### feat: sync tells a fast-forward from a rewrite

The gate runs before any fetch and holds back every repo with local work, the one whose remote
has not moved and the one whose remote only added commits included. One unpushed bookmark
anywhere in a repo then stops every sync of it, wink's case in iiac-perf, and the look's verdict
there read "held back" over a `main` it had just called up to date.

- Sync asks the remote where every one of its bookmarks is, a fetch bringing all of them, and
  compares with the last fetch. The remote where the last fetch left it means nothing to fetch:
  sync says so, notes the local work, and exits 0.
- When a bookmark moved, its commits are downloaded with no ref moved, and the move is classified
  by ancestry: a fast-forward, a rewrite, new, or deleted.
  - Tried in scratch repos, colocated and not: `git fetch --refmap= --no-tags
    --no-write-fetch-head <remote> <ref>` brought the remote's commit into the object store, left
    every git ref as it was, and jj saw nothing, no bookmark, `@`, or remote-tracking ref changed
    and no operation added, a later jj command included. `--refmap=` is what does it: without
    it git moves the remote-tracking ref as a side effect, and jj imports that as a fetch.
  - The ancestry walk is gix's, in-process: `rev_walk` is in the build as it is, where
    `merge_base` wants a feature jj-lib does not turn on. A revset cannot ask, jj not having
    imported the remote's commit.
  - It is a second form of the one spawn, under the same register entry, and both go through one
    function so the `#[allow]` is at one site.
- A fast-forward replaces nothing, so no local work can be moved by it: sync fetches, and says
  what it leaves untouched. Untouched is not brought up to date: an `@` with changes, or an
  unpushed bookmark, stays on the old commit, and moving it is the user's act.
- Two things still hold a repo back, each reported with its bookmark:
  - A bookmark that moved on the remote has local commits of its own, the fetch leaving it
    conflicted. This is any bookmark, not the synced one alone.
  - The remote rewrote or deleted a bookmark and the repo holds local work. Which commits the
    rewrite replaced is not worked out: any local work is taken as at risk, the check erring
    toward holding.
- The look and the sync share the finding out, `look_repos`, so the look's verdict and the sync's
  act cannot disagree. In the scratch scenarios each verdict was borne out by the sync run after
  it.
- A look now downloads, where the second rung's fetched nothing at all: the moved bookmarks'
  commits land in the git store with no ref naming them. They are the commits a fetch would
  bring.
- `--force` is the flag's documented name, wink's call, `--rebase` staying as an alias: past the
  gate there is often nothing to rebase, and "force a sync" is what the flag is reached for.
- Every sync now spawns git once to ask, and once more when the remote moved, where the look
  alone did.

##### feat: sync is safe by default closing

Closing out the cycle. Close-out shape: trapezoid.

- The cycle changed its design five times after it opened, and each change was found by trying
  the last one.
  - A dry run that put a bookmark back, a restore of the whole repo, a gate on local work alone,
    a look that asked the remote, and the gate that tells a fast-forward from a rewrite.
  - What moved it each time was a trial in scratch repos or wink running the built binary in
    another project, never the plan. The acceptance check written at the opening tested the
    first design and would have passed it.
- The plan could have been cheaper to change. The record was rewritten whole four times, and a
  rung's worth of code was written and discarded twice.
  - A trial of the mechanism before the ladder is written would have found the first two faults
    in an hour: a fetch moves a bookmark, and a restore is blind to the remote afterwards.
- A project rule was learned by tripping it: the ban on spawning git, met when clippy stopped
  the build and after the agent had said the spawn added nothing new.
  - The register in `clippy.toml` is where to look before a `Command::new` is written.
- A go was misread once, "option 1" taken to mean the body as it stood, and a published commit
  was re-described in both repos to add the legend line.
  - A choice that changes what is pushed is worth restating in the words of its effect before
    the push.
- The trial of this file is the subject of the Todo entry that makes it the rule, and what the
  trial showed is written there.

content.text:
`vc-x1 sync --dry-run` leaves them out on purpose, so the way to find them is a jj revset:

```
jj log -r 'visible_heads() ~ ::(bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()) ~ @'
```

It lists every visible head that no local or remote bookmark reaches, leaving out the working copy. Run just now in the work-repo, it prints the same three the notes named:

| Commit | Date | Title |
|---|---|---|
| `2fbd6c40` | 2026-09-04 | agent-files(adoption): v0.2.0 (marked divergent) |
| `b34cb7b3` | 2026-08-04 | refactor: trapezoid-push + body-intro validation opening |
| `7694fce7` | 2026-07-20 | refactor: extract push/state.rs |

That shows only the heads. To see everything that hangs off them, including any commits beneath a head that are also unreachable, use:

```
jj log -r 'mutable() ~ ::(bookmarks() | remote_bookmarks()) ~ @'
```

The sync look skips them because the cycle decided a check that counted them would hold the repo back for good over commits no sync moves.

If you want them gone, `jj abandon <rev>` hides each one, and `jj op log` can still bring it back. I have not abandoned anything.

The plain version: sync only looks at bookmarks, so commits with no bookmark are found with the jj revset above, and the three old ones are still there.

11	## Prose form
12	
13	([why](rationale.md#prose-form))
14	
15	Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro that explains the *why* or
16	the high-level *what*, sharpened to a *problem statement* where a surface calls for one (see
17	[Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape)), then a `-` bullet list for the details. The width
18	numbers and the wrap discipline live in [Line widths](#line-widths) below, their one home. One fact
19	per bullet or sub-bullet beats a paragraph packing several. Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs: they
20	hide the structure that bullets make scannable. Punctuation that joins clauses without naming their
21	relationship is the same failure at sentence scale. See [Semicolons](#semicolons) and [Typeable
22	punctuation only](#typeable-punctuation-only).
23	
24	Surfaces that use this shape:
25	
26	- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files. See [Doc
27	  comments](code.md#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
28	- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and agent-repo). The title is the commit-specific add-on.
29	  See [The per-rung flow](../AGENTS.md#the-per-rung-flow).
30	- The cycle-record, `TODO.md > ## In Progress`. See [The In Progress
31	  block](notes.md#the-in-progress-block).
32	- Todo entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are
33	  still fine.
34	
35	Bullet *content* differs by surface:
36	
37	- **Commit bodies**: the [Problem-first shape](#problem-first-shape) for finished work, arranged by
38	  [Commit-body form](#commit-body-form) below. What is specific to a commit:
39	  - the problem statement defines any word the title assumes, since the title is what a reader meets
40	    first and it answers the problem
41	  - **no file list.** The diff and `git show --stat` are the mechanical record, so restating them is
42	    a second copy that can drift from the first. An import of a thousand files is one change
43	  - these are claims a reader has to follow, so they are sentences rather than fragments. A bullet
44	    wanting a paragraph belongs in the cycle-record instead
45	  - the **deliberation** stays out: alternatives weighed, evidence, dates, costs accepted. Those
46	    live in the cycle-record, the `## Todo` entry, and the session the `ochid:` trailer names, each
47	    reachable from the commit by construction. The problem itself is a *why* and belongs here
48	- **Cycle-record / todo**: bullets are conceptual (design points, structural notes, the "what landed
49	  and why" at a notch above file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list. The diff
50	  is the mechanical record, the commit body the problem and solution, the cycle-record the design
51	  thinking, and none restates another.
52	- **Doc comments**: bullets are whatever structure fits (fields, cases, invariants).
53	
54	### Leads are labels, unmarked
55	
56	In a list item or a numbered step, a lead is a short label ending in a colon, with no markup, and
57	the sentence after it is complete without it:
58	
59	```
60	1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
61	```
62	
63	- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
64	  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
65	  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
66	  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
67	  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
68	- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
69	  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
70	  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
71	  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
72	  renumbering.
73	- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
74	  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
75	- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
76	  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
77	  (wink, 2026-08-21).
78	- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.
79	
80	### One spelling per term
81	
82	A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
83	`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
84	spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
85	where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.
86	
87	### Bullet form
88	
89	A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
90	is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
91	the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
92	recast so the name is not the first word.
93	
94	### Line widths
95	
96	Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
97	restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
98	when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.
99	
100	- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
101	- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
102	  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
103	- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
104	- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
105	  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.
106	
107	The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
108	touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
109	narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
110	row, indented code in a comment).
111	
112	### Problem-first shape
113	
114	`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
115	shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.
116	
117	- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
118	  follows it.
119	- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
120	  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
121	  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
122	- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
123	  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
124	    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
125	    `(done)` form.
126	  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
127	    into a cycle.
128	
129	**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
130	writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
131	body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
132	is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
133	was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
134	opening what it intended to do.

1. Backfill: fill every as-built ladder whose commits have landed, before anything else.
```

- Label names, sentence instructs: a reader's eye takes bold at the head of an item as the item's
  name and resumes at the plain text expecting a full sentence, so a bold lead that is the
  sentence's own verb or subject (`**Backfill** every as-built ladder ...`) loses its imperative to
  the reader who skips it. Measured 2026-08-21, at the review of the rule that example is from: the
  reviewer read "every as-built ladder" and stopped, with nothing telling them what to do.
- The inverted case: a rule stated in bold is the same failure inverted. When the bold is a whole
  sentence and the plain text is commentary, the reader who skips bold reads the commentary as the
  rule. The fix is the same: a short name as the label, the rule as the plain sentence. The hard
  rules in AGENTS.md are the instance, and the names they gained are greppable and survive a
  renumbering.
- Definitions: the same shape, `Term: what it means.` A period after a bold term (`**Term.** ...`)
  reads as a heading, which is the label reading again.
- No markup on the label: bold is what makes the eye treat the lead as a heading and skip it, and
  the agent-files are read by an agent, which needs no emphasis. The colon alone marks the label
  (wink, 2026-08-21).
- The price: one word of redundancy, paid on purpose: the label is skippable, the sentence is not.

### One spelling per term

A defined term has one spelling, everywhere: `work-repo` and `agent-repo` are always hyphenated,
`agent-files`, `version-of-record`, `dual-repo`, and `as-built` likewise, and no rule varies the
spelling by how the term is used. Terminology in AGENTS.md defines the terms, and this section is
where the spelling rule lives, since a glossary is read for meaning rather than for spelling.

### Bullet form

A bullet is a full sentence, capitalized and ending in a period or question mark, unless the list
is a plain list of things (files, names, options), which takes neither. A list is all one or all
the other. A sentence never opens with a lower-case name (`squash-push`, `rationale.md`), it is
recast so the name is not the first word.

### Line widths

Every width number lives here and nowhere else: the other files and sections link here rather than
restating one, so a change is a single edit and the copies cannot drift. Consolidated 2026-08-09,
when the body width moved and the restatements had to be hunted.

- **Prose**, all durable text: wrap at <=100 cols, bullet continuations indented two spaces.
- **Source**, doc comments and inline comments included: <=100 cols, which is rustfmt's default
  `max_width` (enforcement notes in [code.md](code.md#line-width)).
- **Commit titles**: <=50 chars.
- **Commit bodies**: <=75 cols, the Linux kernel patch standard. It replaced git's older 72
  convention here 2026-08-09, and published bodies keep the wrap they shipped with.

The widths are wrap defaults, not absolutes (the title cap excepted). Existing text re-wraps when
touched, no mass sweeps. Write to the full width: wrap near the limit rather than imitating the
narrow wrap of older text, and a line that reads better long stays long (an URL, a literal report
row, indented code in a comment).

### Problem-first shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, `## Todo` entries, and commit bodies use a sharper form of the same
shape: a problem, then how it is answered, then the steps that get there.

- **Problem statement** (the why): one or two sentences. Don't pad with intent, don't restate what
  follows it.
- **Solution statement** (the what/how): what is done about the problem, in broad terms, answering
  whatever question the problem statement raises. Surface-specific rules are in [Bullet content
  differs by surface](#prose-form) above.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when), the steps. Formality differs by surface:
  - In Progress: a committed ladder, one step per commit. See [Conventional-commit
    shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit) for the per-step title + `(current)` /
    `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering, formalized only when the entry is picked up
    into a cycle.

**Timing decides whether the solution statement is provisional, not whether it is written.** A cycle
writes one at Preparation, before the work, and revises it as steps land. The close-out's commit
body carries the final one. A `## Todo` entry's is provisional in the same way. Only a commit body's
is settled, because a commit is finished by the time it has one. The earlier rule here said a plan
was for work not yet done and a solution for work that is, which left a cycle unable to say at its
opening what it intended to do.

136	### sync --undo takes back the last sync
137	
138	(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) A sync that was forced with `--force` and is regretted, or that stopped
139	part-way on a conflict, has no easy way back. `vc-x1 sync --undo` would put a repo back the way
140	the last sync found it: its bookmarks, `@`, its files, and what jj believes the remote holds.
141	
142	Deferred from the cycle **feat: sync is safe by default**, where it was a rung and was dropped
143	before any code was written. That cycle made the routine sync safe by itself, so undo serves the
144	forced sync alone, and its design turned out to hold more than the cycle had room for.
145	
146	The complications, the plain version:
147	
148	- jj's own undo is not enough. `jj op restore` puts jj's records back and leaves git's own note
149	  of where the remote is at the new value. jj then believes it has already seen the remote's
150	  change and never follows it again, so the repo says "up to date" when it is not.
151	  - A real undo puts git's note back as well, so the next sync sees the remote's move and does
152	    its work again.
153	  - This part is written and was tested: `restore_as_found`, with its tests, in
154	    `tmp/rung1-restore-draft/` on wink's machine. `tmp/` is not committed, so it should be
155	    brought into the repo, or rewritten from this description, when the entry is picked up.
156	- Undo has to know where the last sync began. The plan is for sync to label each jj operation it
157	  makes, and for undo to read jj's operation log back to the latest labelled one.
158	  - Nothing is saved in a file of our own. A saved snapshot that went stale is what had the old
159	    `revert` command removed at 0.78.3.
160	  - Every step of a sync then has to run through one place that adds the label. Today moving
161	    `@` at the end of a sync does not.
162	- Work done after the sync must not be thrown away. If anything but plain saves of the working
163	  copy came after it, a commit, a bookmark move, another sync, an earlier undo, then going back
164	  would discard that work. Undo refuses and lists what is in the way.
165	- The conversation is the hard case. In the agent-repo a running session writes its transcript
166	  all the time, and putting files back to an earlier state would wipe the lines written since.
167	  - So undo carries later writes forward: it works out what changed since the sync and puts
168	    that on top of the restored state.
169	  - A file the sync never touched is then not rewritten at all, which is what keeps a live
170	    transcript safe.
171	  - A file that both the sync and later work changed has no clean answer, and undo refuses
172	    before it changes anything.
173	- A second undo in a row refuses, the first being work done after the sync.
174	
175	Not yet decided, wink's to say:
176	
177	- Whether "only saves of the working copy may follow" is the right rule for refusing, or an
178	  `--undo --force` should exist. Past that point `jj op restore` may be the honest tool.
179	- Whether later writes are carried forward as above, or undo refuses whenever any file changed
180	  since. Refusing is simpler and makes undo nearly unusable in the agent-repo during a session.
181	- Whether each repo is undone by itself from its own log, or both repos of one sync run go back
182	  together or not at all.
183	
184	Smaller parts of the design:
185	
186	- `--undo --dry-run` says what an undo would do, or why it would refuse, and changes nothing.
187	- A sync that changed something ends by naming `vc-x1 sync --undo`, and so does the report of one
188	  that stopped part-way, in place of the bare `jj op restore` it prints today.
189	- The scope is `-R` and `--scope`, as a sync takes them.
190	- What jj-lib offers was checked at 0.45.1: attributes on an operation, a marker on a snapshot
191	  operation, and a three-way merge of trees.

  - A file that both the sync and later work changed has no clean answer, and undo refuses
    before it changes anything.
- A second undo in a row refuses, the first being work done after the sync.

Not yet decided, wink's to say:

- Whether "only saves of the working copy may follow" is the right rule for refusing, or an
  `--undo --force` should exist. Past that point `jj op restore` may be the honest tool.
- Whether later writes are carried forward as above, or undo refuses whenever any file changed
  since. Refusing is simpler and makes undo nearly unusable in the agent-repo during a session.
- Whether each repo is undone by itself from its own log, or both repos of one sync run go back
  together or not at all.

Smaller parts of the design:

- `--undo --dry-run` says what an undo would do, or why it would refuse, and changes nothing.
- A sync that changed something ends by naming `vc-x1 sync --undo`, and so does the report of one
  that stopped part-way, in place of the bare `jj op restore` it prints today.
- The scope is `-R` and `--scope`, as a sync takes them.
- What jj-lib offers was checked at 0.45.1: attributes on an operation, a marker on a snapshot
  operation, and a three-way merge of trees.

vc-x1 0.84.21 - jj workspace tooling

Usage: vc-x1 [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]

Commands:
  agent-files       The agent-files set: its version, and a diff against a copy
                    of it
  version           Print vc-x1, jj-lib, and jj-data versions
  chid              Print the changeID for a revision
  desc              Show full description of a commit
  list              List commits in a jj repo
  show              Show commit details and diff summary
  status            Working-copy status and clean verdict, by scope (alias st)
  lookup            Show the lines in the other repo that a line in this one
                    relates to
  agent-session     Display an agent session transcript as a conversation
  validate          Run the workspace's configured validation commands
  validate-agent    Check the agent repo is published (main matches main@origin)
  validate-desc     Validate commit descriptions against the other repo
  fix-desc          Fix commit descriptions against the other repo (dry-run by
                    default)
  validate-config   Check the workspace's config files
  validate-anchors  Check a markdown record's own anchors and references
  validate-todo     Check todo-file entry numbering and indent
  fix-todo          Renumber todo-file entries (dry-run by default)
  clone             Clone a dual-repo project
  init              Create a new dual-repo project
  symlink           Create Claude Code project symlink
  sync              Fetch and sync a set of repos to their remotes
  squash-push       Squash SOURCE into TARGET, advance a bookmark, and push
  config            Print settable config keys and their defaults
  push              Commit both repos, push the work repo, squash-push the bot
                    repo
  help              Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

The `agent-files(proposal): v0.2.8` entry is reworded: it stays parked on your word of 2026-10-11 until `zDOING.md` and `zTODO.md` are settled, the sync cycle it waited on has landed, and it wants a rebase and its `TODO.md` reconciled when it resumes. Uncommitted, like the rest.

## Rename and delete

Your entry says "Rename work or agent repos handling .vc-config.{toml|md}". This is what I think each command has to touch, from `init`'s steps and this workspace's config, as a starting point.

**What a workspace's name is written into**

| Where | Example here | Rename | Delete |
|---|---|---|---|
| Work-repo directory | `vc-x1/` | move | remove |
| Agent-repo directory | `.agent-session` inside it | unchanged when nested, moved when it sits elsewhere | remove |
| GitHub repos | `vc-x1`, `vc-x1.agent-session` | rename both | delete both, irreversible |
| `origin` URL in each repo | https URL built from the name | rewrite | n/a |
| `.vc-config.md`, both sides | `[remote] agent-repo`, `[family] member` | edit, which is a commit in each repo | n/a |
| Claude Code symlink | `~/.claude/projects/<mangled path>` | old one removed, new one made | remove |

**Things that make rename harder than it looks**

- **The config edit is a commit:** the name is in committed files, so a rename ends with a commit in both repos, which should be cross-linked like any other.
- **A live session breaks:** the symlink and Claude Code's project name come from the directory path, so a rename run from inside a session moves the ground under it. I think it has to refuse, or be run with no session open.
- **Siblings hold the name too:** the template and messages repos, and other members' configs, refer to a member by name. I would leave those out and have the command list them.

**Things that make delete dangerous**

- **Remote deletion cannot be undone:** I'd make it dry-run by default, as `fix-desc` is, with local and remote deletion as separate flags.
- **Unpushed work:** deleting the local side while keeping the remote should refuse when either repo holds commits the remote lacks.
- **Half-made workspaces:** the "init refuses a name GitHub would change" entry notes `init` has no undo and leaves an empty public repo and a local workspace with no remote. Delete would have to work on those, not only on complete workspaces.

**My suggestion**

Do delete first. It is the smaller command, it gives `init` the cleanup it lacks, and it forces the "find every part of a workspace from its config" code that rename then reuses.

**Questions that decide the shape**

1. What prompted this: cleaning up test workspaces from `init`, or renaming real projects?
2. Does rename take the whole workspace together, or one side at a time as your note reads? One side alone overlaps the "repos.agent becomes repos.agent-dir" entry.
3. Is `.vc-config.toml` still a live format these commands must handle, or is `.md` the only one?

The plain version: a workspace's name lives in six places, delete is the simpler and more dangerous command and should come first, and rename needs to end in a commit and cannot run under a live session.

Both decisions are now bullets in the "Add a rename and delete subcommands" entry, dated and attributed to you. I also fixed the "Renanme" typo in your line. The reason given for the rename refusal is mine: a rename moves the directory path that the Claude Code symlink and project name are built from. Reword it if yours was different.

Your two decisions open three questions, which I recorded in the entry as open:

1. **How rename knows an agent is running.** I see three ways:
   - **Process check:** look for a process whose working directory is inside the workspace. It needs no cooperation from the agent, but it reads `/proc`, so it is Linux-only.
   - **Recent writes:** treat a session file in the agent-repo modified in the last few minutes as a live session. It is portable, but it is a guess: an idle session passes and a just-closed one blocks.
   - **Lock file:** the agent takes a lock at acquaint and releases it at exit, like the messages repo's `owner`. It is exact, but a session that dies leaves a stale lock for you to clear.

   I'd take the process check, with `--force` for when it is wrong.
2. **Whether rename renames the GitHub repos.** With delete leaving the remote alone, the consistent choice is that rename does too: it changes the local side, prints the two `gh repo rename` commands, and updates the `origin` URLs to the new names. The other choice is that rename does it all, since a half-renamed workspace pushes to a URL that only works through GitHub's redirect.
3. **Whether delete refuses over unpushed work.** Since the remote is now the only surviving copy after a delete, I think it should refuse when either repo holds commits or uncommitted changes the remote lacks, with `--force` to override.

One thing I noticed in the file: the two entries under this one, "symlink names a path over 200 characters as Claude Code does" and "init refuses a name GitHub would change", are now `####` headings, which makes them read as parts of the rename and delete entry. If that grouping is not intended, they want `###` again.

content.text:
Thoughts only, nothing edited.

**1. Lock file `.agent.running`**

- **Who writes it is the real question.** If the agent writes it at acquaint, it is a rule in the agent-files, so it is a convention cycle and every adopter needs it before rename can trust the file. If a Claude Code session-start and session-end hook writes it, no agent cooperation is needed, but it only covers Claude Code.
- **Stale locks:** a session that dies leaves the file behind. Putting the process id in it lets rename check whether that process is still alive and clear a dead lock itself, which avoids the messages repo's "only a human can tell" problem.
- **More than one session:** two sessions in one workspace need a line each, or the first to exit removes the other's lock.
- **Existing workspaces:** `init` can write the ignore line for new ones, but current adopters need it added, the same kind of chore as the stale `/.vc-x1` ignore line already in the Todo.
- **Delete should honour it too.** Removing a workspace under a live session is as bad as renaming it.

**2. Rename handles remotes**

I read "if we can assume it won't be deleted" as: since delete never removes a remote, rename can count on the remote being there. Tell me if you meant something else.

- **Order:** remote first. If the GitHub rename fails (name taken, no permission), nothing local has changed. GitHub redirects the old URL, so each later step can still push if the run stops part-way.
- **Sequence I'd expect:** rename both GitHub repos, rewrite both `origin` URLs, edit the configs, commit and push, move the directory, remake the symlink.
- **No remote, or not GitHub:** a local-only workspace skips the remote steps. A remote that is not GitHub should refuse and not guess.
- **Dry run:** worth having, printing the steps as `init` does.

**3. Neither proceeds with uncommitted or unpushed work**

- **This is the status verdict.** "Clean" is already defined as both repos' `@` empty, and the status entry plans a per-repo verdict function that also carries publish state. Rename and delete should call that, not have their own check.

content.text:
Thoughts on each, nothing edited. These three decisions are not yet in the Todo entry.

**1. The lock file as a counted mutex**

- **The count needs its own guard.** Two sessions starting together can both read 0 and both write 1. The update has to be a read-change-write under a file lock, or one session's exit deletes the file while the other is still running.
- **A count cannot heal after a crash.** A session that dies never decrements, so the file stays at 1 or more forever, and nothing in a number says which holder is dead. Recovery is then you deleting the file by hand, or rename taking an override. Process ids would have let the tool tell; a count trades that away for simplicity.
- **A command should own it.** If the agent edits the count by hand, a slip leaves it wrong. Something like a `vc-x1` subcommand that takes and releases the lock would do the guarded update, and it is what a session-start and session-end hook would call.
- **Rename and delete only need existence.** The file being there means refuse; the count matters only to the releasing side, to know when to remove it.

**2. The remote cannot be lost**

I agree. A GitHub rename either happens or is refused, so the repo exists under the old name or the new one. What can still go wrong is smaller:

- **A name GitHub would alter.** The entry "init refuses a name GitHub would change" covers GitHub silently turning other characters into `-`. Rename should run that same check on the new name, or our rewritten `origin` URL points at a name GitHub did not use.
- **Stopping between the two repos.** If the work-repo renames and the agent-repo's rename is refused, the workspace is half-renamed. Rename should be safe to run again: it sees which repo already has the new name and continues from there.

**3. Warnings and the confirm**

So there are two tiers: uncommitted or unpushed work on a bookmark is a refusal, and bookmarkless commits or a half-made workspace are warnings that need `--yes` or a `Y` at the prompt.

- **The half-made case needs a precise line.** In a repo with no remote, everything is unpushed, including `main`. The rule would read: a repo with a remote and unpushed work refuses, and a repo with no remote at all warns. Uncommitted changes in a no-remote repo would warn too, I assume.
- **The prompt should say what goes.** For delete, list the directories and the symlink to be removed and the commits that exist nowhere else, then ask, with No as the default.
- **An agent has no terminal.** It would use `--yes`, as it does for push, with your go in the conversation standing in for the prompt.
- **Rename probably needs neither warning.** Bookmarkless commits move with the directory, and a workspace with no remote just skips the remote steps. The warnings look like delete's alone.

message.content: 1. I thought linux had a notion of a "owned" file that was managed by one process at a time?

content.text:
Yes, Linux has that: it is the advisory file lock, `flock`, and it changes the picture for the lock file.

**What it is**

- **A lock a process holds on an open file.** One process can hold it exclusively, or many can hold it shared. Another process asking for a conflicting lock either waits or is told no.
- **The kernel releases it when the holder goes away.** When the process exits, crashes, or is killed, its open files close and the lock is gone. Nothing is left to clean up.
- **It is advisory, not ownership.** Nothing stops a process that does not ask for the lock from reading, writing or deleting the file. It works because every tool that cares asks first. Linux once had a mandatory form and removed it.

**Why it fits better than a counter**

- **No stale lock.** This is the crash problem I raised about the count: a dead session's lock disappears by itself.
- **The kernel does the counting.** Each session holds a shared lock for as long as it runs. Rename and delete try for the exclusive lock without waiting, and are refused while any session holds a shared one. The file needs no contents and never needs deleting.
- **It is in Rust's standard library**, and it works on macOS as well as Linux.

**The catch**

The lock lasts only as long as the process holding it. A `vc-x1` command the agent runs exits in a moment and the lock goes with it. So something has to stay alive for the whole session and hold the file open:

- **A holder process started at session start**, by a hook or the agent, that sits there holding the shared lock. It then has to die when the session does, or a leftover holder blocks rename the way a stale count would. Linux can tie a child's life to its parent's, which would do it, but that part is Linux-only.
- **Claude Code itself holding it** would be ideal, and we do not control that.

A lighter use is also possible: keep your counter, and take the lock only for the moment of each update. That fixes two sessions racing on the count, but not the crash case.

The plain version: Linux file locks free themselves when their holder dies, which removes the stale-lock problem, but they need one process that lives exactly as long as the session, and arranging that is the hard part.

That works as a first experiment, and the existing rules already support it: Acquaint step 1 says to read `custom.md` and do what it asks at acquaint, so one line there is enough to make every session take the lock.

**The agent cannot hold the lock itself.** Each command I run is a process that exits, and the lock goes with it. So "the agent takes the lock" has to mean one of two things:

- **The agent starts a holder in the background** at acquaint, for example `flock -s .agent.running sleep infinity`. The holder keeps the shared lock for the session, and there is no release step to forget.
- **The agent edits the counter** at acquaint and again before exit. This needs no background process, but a session closed without warning never decrements.

I'd try the holder first, because a release the agent must remember is the part most likely to fail. You often end a session by closing it, and I get no turn to clean up.

**What the experiment has to find out**

- **Does the holder die with the session?** I believe background commands are killed when Claude Code exits, but I have not verified it, and the sandbox may change the answer. If it survives, it blocks rename like a stale count.
- **What happens on a crash or a killed terminal**, as opposed to a clean exit.
- **A resumed session.** A session continued without a fresh acquaint would hold no lock, since the holder from before is gone.
- **Whether the check works by hand.** Until rename exists, `flock -xn .agent.running true` from another terminal stands in for it: it should fail while a session is open and succeed after.

**Two points on where the rule goes**

- **It is an agent-file change**, so it is its own commit, separate from today's `TODO.md` edits.
- **The agent-files are in mild tension with themselves here.** One rule says `custom.md` is for experimenting in one file; another says an adopter that edits the agent-files directly, as this project does, keeps `custom.md` to pointers only. A one-line experiment with a note saying it is one seems within the spirit, and it is your call.

The `.gitignore` line for `.agent.running` goes in with it.

I did not change the link, because it is correct: the fault is in `validate-anchors`, and it is already recorded as bugs 15 and 19 in `notes/bugs.md`.

- **The link is right.** GitHub strips the backticks from "Support POR workspaces in `push`" and keeps the text, so the anchor is `#support-por-workspaces-in-push`, which is what the link uses.
- **The checker is wrong.** It drops the code span's text when it builds the slug, so it computes `#support-por-workspaces-in` and reports the working link as broken. Bug 19 notes that its "did you mean" suggestion invites exactly the edit that would break the link on GitHub.

There are two ways to make the check pass:

- **Fix the checker.** Bug 19's fix direction is to strip the backticks and keep the span's text. That is a code change, so it is a cycle of its own, and it clears every heading that names code, not just this one.
- **Take the backticks out of the heading**, making it "Support POR workspaces in push". Both slugs then agree and the check passes today, at the cost of the heading no longer marking `push` as a command. Other backticked headings would stay affected if they are linked.

I'd fix the checker. Which do you want?

(wink + agent, 2026-10-11) A heading holding a code span is slugged as though the span's text
